diagnosis_plain: Bilateral Hip Dysplasia — OFA Grade Moderate, with early secondary osteoarthritis

pet.chief_complaint: 3-month hind limb lameness, worse on right side; difficulty with stairs; morning stiffness
pet.history: No prior joint complaints; lameness onset 3 months ago, gradually worsening

summary.severity: Significant concern — bilateral structural damage, surgical window now optimal
summary.decision_window: Urgent — 2-year-old is at peak surgical benefit window
summary.prognosis: Excellent with THR; good with FHO; progressive deterioration without surgery
summary.priority_match: THR best matches active lifestyle; Conservative viable if budget is the constraint
summary.next_step: Consult orthopedic surgeon for THR candidacy evaluation; right hip priority

findings.name: Norberg Angle (Right Hip)
findings.meaning: Significantly below normal — poor femoral head coverage, primary HD criterion

findings.name: Acetabular Depth
findings.meaning: Inadequate coverage of femoral head — classic radiographic sign of HD

findings.name: OFA Grade (Overall)
findings.meaning: Joint cartilage and structure already damaged; intervention warranted

paths.label: Option A
paths.survival: Symptom control only; arthritis will inevitably progress
paths.aligns: Low upfront cost; no surgical risk; buys time while planning
paths.tensions: Does not correct underlying structure; surgery likely needed within 5–8 years with worse outcomes

paths.label: Option B
paths.survival: Excellent outcomes when performed within age window — limited applicability here
paths.aligns: Best for dogs under 18 months; less applicable at 2 years
paths.tensions: Skeletal maturity reduces benefit; secondary arthritis may limit results

paths.label: Option C
paths.survival: >90% achieve good to excellent outcomes; near-normal function at 5+ years
paths.aligns: Best long-term prognosis for active 28 kg dog; implant lifespan covers most of dog's life
paths.tensions: Highest upfront cost; implant loosening / infection risk <3%; strict candidate screening required

paths.label: Option D
paths.survival: 70–80% satisfactory in large breeds; limited mobility compared to THR
paths.aligns: Budget-friendly surgical option; pain relief without implant
paths.tensions: Creates false joint; activity level and gait may be permanently reduced in large dogs

prognosis_bullets: THR: >90% of dogs achieve good to excellent outcomes; long-term function approaches normal dogs at 5+ years
FHO: ~70–80% of large-breed dogs achieve satisfactory results, though gait and intensity may be somewhat limited
Conservative management: effective symptom control, but arthritis inevitably progresses; surgery typically needed within 5–8 years
Untreated moderate HD: ~40% develop significantly worsened pain within 5 years, requiring more aggressive intervention
prognosis_note: At 2 years old, this dog is at the optimal surgical window — skeletal maturity is complete but arthritis has not yet advanced severely. Acting now maximizes surgical benefit. Delaying increases arthritis severity and reduces long-term outcomes.
questions: Given the current arthritis level, is conservative management still viable as a bridge before surgery?
If we choose THR, how many procedures does your team perform annually? Which implant system do you use (BioMedtrix, Kyon, etc.)?
For bilateral HD, do you recommend treating both hips simultaneously or staged? Typical interval between procedures?
What pre-surgical workup is required (cardiac evaluation, bloodwork)? Any contraindications to screen for?
What does the post-THR rehabilitation protocol look like? Is hydrotherapy or physical therapy available?
If we start with conservative management, can long-term NSAID use accelerate cartilage damage?
sources: Lust G. An overview of the pathogenesis of canine hip dysplasia. J Am Vet Med Assoc. 1997
Olmstead ML. Total hip replacement in the dog. Semin Vet Med Surg. 1987
Off W, Matis U. Excision arthroplasty of the hip joint in dogs and cats. Vet Comp Orthop Traumatol. 2010
